newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ravers groove, sweat in sunny Berlin Love Parade.
newsitem.headline: Ravers groove, sweat in sunny Berlin Love Parade.

text.p: The sun blazed down on the world's largest techno music party on Saturday as an international crowd of up to one million people boogied and sweated through the centre of Berlin for the city's ninth annual Love Parade.

Ravers came from around the world to dance behind 38 brightly decorated floats equipped with turbo-powered sound systems down a six-km (four-mile) stretch of an eight-lane boulevard which leads from the landmark Brandenburg Gate.
"We came because it's something you just have to experience," said Cornelius Hummel, a 19-year-old student from Stuttgart dressed in a Scottish kilt and bug-eyed sunglasses.
"You can't find this kind of euphoria anywhere else," said Karl-Hans Mayer, 50, a Berlin cameraman who has attended the parade nearly every year. "You simply cannot beat it."

As temperatures climbed to almost 30 degrees Celsius, first aid workers said they had treated over one hundred people for dehydration and heatstroke, but added nobody had been seriously injured in the huge crush of dancers.
The annual event, which last year drew 750,000 people, attracts fans of techno, a mix of thundering beats and repetitive electronic riffs supplied by disc jockeys and their enormous sound systems.

"We go to clubs in Holland, but this is the real thing -- the mother of them all," said Sjoerd Ory, 25, a business student from Groningen in the Netherlands. "We are not going to sleep tonight if we can help it."
More than 130 parties were scheduled for Saturday night in Berlin dance clubs, in parks and even on Potsdamer Platz, Europe's largest construction site in the heart of Berlin.
Berlin Interior Minister Joerg Schoenbohm told German television he expected the evening to run smoothly.
"I am optimistic," Schoenbohm said. "I expect the young people will tire themselves out in the clubs tonight and that it will stay peaceful."

Although city officials love the Love Parade for the up to 150 million marks ($84 million) in revenues it is expected to bring this year, it has made a few enemies among nature lovers who object to the heaps of garbage and human waste the crowds create.

The German BUND environmental group tried to re-route the event this year away from the Tiergarten without success and settled for marching along the parade route with huge signs reading "Make Love Not Waste".

Although right- and left-wing extremists had threatened violence and disruption at the huge street party, police reported no disturbances as the dancing, expected to last into the early hours of Sunday, got under way.
A rival "Hate Parade", organised by disc jockeys who opposed the main event's "commercialism" only drew about 500 people and broke up after a few hours.

Before the parade, the asking price for a spot on a float hovered around 3,000 marks and street vendors spent the day hawking everything, from water pistols ravers used to cool each other down, to plastic whistles, the essential rave accessory.
Overcrowded buses, trains and cars with visitors from across Europe bound for the parade caused traffic jams across the country's motorways and up to two-hour delays at Berlin's main train station.

Some new arrivals held an impromptu "rave" on Friday evening in front of the Zoologischer Garten station soon after stepping off the platforms, while 3,000 others hijacked the posh Kurfuerstendamm shopping avenue for an all-night party.

Most accommodation has been booked for weeks with people coming from as far afield as South Africa, Australia and the United States. The Love Parade appears to have become an essential stop on any backpacker's European tour.

Not to be outdone by Berlin, Frankfurt staged a giant open air rock concert in its main shopping avenue, the Zeil, with 300,000 people expected to dance the night away to the rhythm of 50 bands performing on four separate platforms. ($ = 1.78 German Marks)
